string.text: A friendly face on the road is a rare thing these days. We carry grain and good cloth to the markets downriver, and you are welcome at our fire tonight.
Greetings, traveller. Ours is honest trade under the protection of the realm, and if you mean us no harm, we wish you a safe road.
Keep your distance. These goods are bound for our own towns, and our guards are well paid to see that they arrive.
You would rob your own? Take it, then, and may the shame of it ride with you all the way home.
This is a lawful caravan of the realm. Take what you will, but every lord between here and the Sea will learn your name.
Take the goods and be cursed for it. Our captains will hunt you down before the season turns.
Good day to you. It does the heart good to meet one of our own on the market road.
Good day, traveller. We are only taking our harvest to the town, and we have no quarrel with anyone.
Please, let us pass. We have a cart of turnips and a few sacks of barley, and nothing here is worth a soldier's time.
Our grain feeds your own towns. Take it if you must, and the hearths will be colder this winter for it.
We have done you no wrong. Take the cart, then, and may your conscience weigh more than our grain.
Take it and be gone. The lord of these lands will hear of this, and so will the rangers in the hills.
Well met on the road. We carry wool and leather down to Aldburg, and it is good to see one of our own along the way.
Greetings, rider. We are bound for Edoras with hides and good saddlery, and we want no trouble on the way.
Ride wide of us. The road to Edoras is watched by the éoreds of the Mark, and they ride fast.
Riding down your own neighbours on the road? Take it, then, and carry the shame of it back to your hall.
We trusted you on this road. Take what you want, but the Riddermark will hear of it.
Take it, thief. The riders of the Mark will hunt you down before you reach the Fords of Isen.
Good day to you. We are taking barley and cheese to market at Aldburg, if the weather holds.
Peace on you, traveller. We are only bringing our harvest to market, and we want no quarrel.
Stay back from us. One blast of our horn will bring the riders down on you.
You would take bread from your own neighbours? Then take it, and may no good horse ever carry you again.
We took you for a friend of the Mark. Take what you came for and be gone.
Take it, then. The Westfold remembers every raid, and so will the riders who come after you.
Ho there, neighbour! Good cloth, dried fish and a cask or two from the south, and a fair price for one of our own.
Good day to you. We carry honest wares down the river roads and want no trouble, though we will gladly do some trade.
That is near enough. My guards have strung their bows, and there is no trade for you today.
Every market from the Lake to the Sea of Rhûn will hear who robbed their own.
We dealt fairly with you, and this is how you repay it? Take what you will, then, and be named a thief in every hall of the North.
Take it, then, and choke on it. Our kin will come for it before the snows.
Well met, neighbour! We are taking the season's honey and wool to market. Walk with us a way, if you like.
Good day. We are only taking our harvest to market, and we would be glad of a peaceful road.
Leave us be. There is nothing on these carts but grain and wool, and we have families waiting on them.
From you, of all people? Our children will go hungry this winter, and it will be your doing.
We showed you nothing but kindness. Take it and go, and may your own fields fail.
Take it, then. We have rebuilt after worse than you, and we will do it again.
Good to see a hill face on this road. We carry wool and hides down to the valley markets, so take what you need for the journey.
Wool, furs and good hill iron, stranger. Fair coin buys fair goods, and we do not haggle long.
Keep your distance and your hands where we can see them. We carry little worth taking and have less patience.
You would rob your own? The clan chiefs will hear of this, and they will not speak your name kindly again.
So your fair words were a lie. Take it, then, and know that Dunland keeps count of every theft.
One more thief on our roads. Take what you will, and the clans will take it back in blood.
Welcome, friend of the hills. We are bringing barley and cheese to market, and you may share our bread tonight.
We are bound for market with what the hills gave us this year, which is little enough. Pass in peace.
We have nothing for you but sheep and hard words. Let us go on to market.
Shame on you, robbing your own hearth-kin. The elders of the clan will hear of it, and so will the whole glen.
Take it, then. Another hungry winter, and one more name to curse by the fireside.
Thieves on our roads again. Take it and go; the hills will know your face next time.
Peace, friend from home. Our beasts carry spice and silk, and the road is easier in good company.
Greetings, traveller. We trade fairly and travel peacefully, and we hope you will let us do both.
Come no nearer. Our guards are well paid and they know their spears.
The whole South will hear of this, and no well will give you water.
So this is what your friendship is worth. Take it, then, but every merchant from the havens of Umbar to the far jungles will know your face.
Take the goods and choke on them. The serpent banner will have its due for every coin you steal.
Peace to you. We take dates and grain to market, and it gladdens us to meet one of our own on the road.
Good day, traveller. We are only farmers on the way to market, with nothing worth a quarrel.
Please, we are only taking our harvest to market. We have no part in the wars of the great houses.
The elders will hear of this, and the sun will see it too.
We greeted you kindly, and this is how you repay us. May the sun burn your road dry.
Take it, then, and may the heat strike you down before you reach home.
Well met on the road! Come, look over the wagons, and drink the first cup of brew as a guest of my clan.
Greetings, traveller. We carry bronze, hides and steppe horses, and we trade fairly with those who keep the peace.
Keep your hands from your weapons. My guards are riders of the East, and they have killed for less.
From the Sea of Rhûn to the far steppe, the clans will hear how you treat your own wagons.
So your peace was a lie. Take what you want, but the one we serve will come asking for every coin of it.
The wagons will not be given up while one guard still stands. Come and take them if you can.
A face from home! We are bound for market with grain and wool. Ride with us a while if you wish.
Good day to you. We are only farmers of the eastern fields, taking our harvest to sell.
We have no quarrel with you, and nothing worth the taking. Let us pass to the market.
Thieving from your own blood? The elders will spit on your name at every fire in the East.
We took you for a friend. Our chieftain protects these fields, and you will pay for this.
We may be farmers, but our people were warriors first. You will bleed for every sack.
A familiar face on a weary road. We carry wine, fine cloth and the work of our smiths, at the price we keep for our own.
Greetings, traveller. Our wares are few but made with care: cloth, wine and blades of old craft, should any please you.
We know whose banner you follow. Keep your hands from your weapons, and we will pass you by in silence.
This from one of our own? Take it, then, and carry the shame of it for longer than you can imagine.
We had thought better of you. Our goods you may seize, but the trust you break today will not be given again.
Take what you will. Our wardens will learn of this, and they are swift and patient both.
Be welcome among us. We carry honey, herbs and the gleanings of the woods to market; walk with us a while if you wish.
Peace to you, traveller. We are bound for market with what the woods have given us this season.
We are no soldiers, only keepers of the woods and gardens. Let us pass quietly, and we will trouble you not at all.
You would rob your own kin of the little the woods have given? Then take it, and may the trees remember your face.
We offered you peace and you answer with this. Take the baskets, and go from our sight.
Robbing gatherers of herbs and honey is a poor sort of victory. Take them; the woods will grow more long after you are dust.
Hail, cousin! Iron from the deep mines and good work from the forges, bound for honest markets. Ride with us a while if you like.
Good day, traveller. These wagons carry worked steel and silver from the mountains, fair goods for fair coin.
Stay back. We know whose banner you ride under, and every guard here is spoiling for a reason.
You would rob your own kin? The clans will hear of it, and no forge in the mountains will serve you again.
So this is how you repay honest trade. Take it, then, and know the debt will be collected with interest.
Take the goods if you can carry them. Every ingot you steal will be paid back in blood before the year is out.
Well met, cousin. We are taking ore and smithwork down to market, and the road is lighter for a familiar face.
Good day to you. Coal, ore and a few sound blades for the market, if you are buying.
We are only miners carrying ore to market. Leave us be and go about your business.
Our elders will speak your name in the halls, and they will not speak it kindly.
We trusted you on this road. Take what you want, but every one of us will remember your face.
Take it and be cursed. The mountain keeps a long account of thieves, and yours is opened today.
Keep your claws off the cargo, every sack is tribute and every sack is counted. Walk with us a while if you like, the road's safer in a crowd.
Hold there. These wagons haul tribute for the masters, so say your business and keep moving.
Get back, you, or the drivers turn their whips on you instead of the slaves.
Robbing your own lot? The overseers will hear of this, and they'll skin us both for it.
Take it, then, thief. When the masters count the tribute short, they'll come hunting for whoever thinned it.
Grab it and choke on it. Every crate bears the mark, and the masters never forget a theft.
You know the whip as well as we do. Let us by, we're late with the grain and the overseers count the hours.
Please, let us pass. If this grain reaches the overseers late, it's our backs that pay.
Don't hurt us! We only work the fields, and the masters own every sack and every one of us.
You know what happens when the tribute comes up short. May the whip find you before it finds us.
Take it. We get the lash either way, and one more beating hardly matters now.
Take it and be cursed. The masters will flay us for this, and then they'll come looking for you.
Easy now, traveller. You have the look of someone who has known a hungry winter, so you know why we ask for your silver.
There is sense in you. Half of what you carry will do, and you keep the rest for your own hearth.
That will feed the clan until the thaw. Walk safe, and if the horse-lords ask, you saw nobody in these hills.
So be it. We bleed the same as you, and we will soon see who bleeds first.
We take no joy in robbing our own sort, but the clan comes first. Lay your purse on that stone and walk on.
That is the sensible road. A fair share for the clan's pot, and nobody need draw a blade.
Kindly done. There is a fire up by the old cairn if the cold catches you on the road.
Stubborn as a hill goat, then. Draw, and let the heather judge it.
We may fight the same war, but the war does not feed my clan. Your coin, or we settle it here.
Good, we keep the peace between us. Give what is fair and our war-chiefs need never hear of it.
Done. Go back to your camp, and keep your band clear of our sheepfolds.
Then the Shadow will have one servant fewer by nightfall. Take them!
We march against the same enemies when the war-horns sound, but this pass belongs to the clan. Pay the toll like any other.
Wise. A share for the toll, and we go back to hating the same enemies.
Paid in full. When our banners next march the same way, remember the hill clans dealt fairly with you.
Banner or no banner, nobody shames the clan on its own ground. At them!
You ride through hills that were stolen from us once already. Every coin you carry is owed to Dunland twice over.
So you can bargain. Empty that purse, all of it, and count yourself lucky we leave you your boots.
Go, and tell whoever you serve that the hill clans still remember.
Good. I would rather take your silver off a corpse. Bring them down!
A long way from home, stranger, and far from any help. The clans have waited years to make one of you pay.
Then it will cost you dearly. Every coin in that purse, and be glad we ask no more.
One purse does not pay off an old grievance. Get out of the hills before we change our minds.
We hoped you would say that. For Dunland and the old wrongs!
Hold your blade! We are only hungry hill clans, and we have done you no wrong. Leave us be and go your way.
Why turn on us? We share the same cold and the same short years, and there is nothing here worth the killing.
You strike at those who fight your own war? The war-chiefs will hear of this treachery.
Back off! We answer the same war-horns as you. Turn your blades on the horse-lords instead.
So someone sends their dogs into our hills now. Come on, then, and learn how the clans fight.
Spare us your fine words. We know why you came, and the heather will hide your bones as well as any.
Enough of my clan has died today. Face me alone, blade to blade, and let the winner take what is left.
We fight the same war, yet here you stand in my hold with my clan's blood on your blade. Fight me alone and settle it.
You have come deep into Dunland to die. Step forward and face the chief of this clan alone, if you have the stomach.
Rein in, traveller. The grass is wide, but every trail across it has a keeper, and the keeper of this one wants your silver.
You see sense. A third of your purse, and we will not trouble your wagons.
It is enough. Ride on, and drink to us if you ever reach the vineyards of Dorwinion.
Then we ride. Make your peace with the sky.
The herds were thin this year and the camp must eat. Hand down your silver and we part without a quarrel.
A good answer. Give what a herder gives a neighbour in a bad season, and we call it even.
The camp will eat tonight because of you. Go in peace while the wind is at your back.
A pity. Strike the drums, and let the steppe decide.
We fight the same war in the end, but the Warlord takes a share of everything that crosses these plains. Pay it.
Good. A fair tithe, and the Eye need not hear that two of its servants quarrelled.
Paid. Take your band on, and keep it clear of our herds.
Then the Dark Lord will have a few servants fewer by dusk. Loose!
Our wagons roll west under the same Shadow as yours, yet these plains keep their own law. Silver for the crossing.
Spoken like a sensible ally. Name a sum worth my time and we will not haggle long.
Our quarrel is settled. Save your anger for the Free Peoples and their walls.
Allies who will not pay are no allies of mine. Ride them down!
A stranger on the Warlord's steppe, and alone. Your silver first, and then we will see what else you are worth.
You bargain like a captive already. Everything in your purse, and the finest thing in your pack besides.
Crawl back the way you came and tell them the East is stirring.
Good. The Warlord pays well for enemy heads. Surround them!
You wandered too far from your friends. Leave your silver here, and perhaps the vultures go hungry today.
Then pay as an enemy pays: every coin, and quickly.
Take your empty purse and go. When next we meet, there will be no bargaining.
Then the drums speak for us. For Rhûn and the Warlord!
Hold! We are horse herders with lean ponies and empty bellies, like any who live by the road. Let us pass.
Why draw on us? The same sun burns us and the same winters starve us. There is no glory in this.
Lower your weapons! We ride under the same Shadow, and the Warlord will hear who broke faith.
You would spill the blood of the Dark Lord's own riders? Turn back before this becomes a feud.
So you come hunting on our grass. Good, my bow has been idle too long.
A long ride for a short life, stranger. Every rider here has sworn to bring your head to the Warlord.
You have fought well enough to earn my respect. Meet me alone, as the old riders did, and the winner keeps the camp.
We stand on the same side of this war, and still you burn my camp. Face me alone, and let the steppe judge which of us is stronger.
Your road ends at my fire, stranger. Leave your riders and face me alone, as the steppe has always settled such things.
Peace, child of the long road. You thirst under the same sun as we do, so you know how this goes. A share of your silver, and we part as friends.
Good. Between travellers of the same hard road there is no need for spears. Offer what is fair and we will not haggle long.
It is done, and no blood spilled under the sun. Drink at the oasis to the east and tell them the raiders sent you.
Then you have chosen badly. Spears level, and let it be quick.
Rest your beasts a moment, traveller. We have little but our spears and a long thirst, and you look like someone who knows what that is. Leave a share of your coin with us.
I thought you would understand. Count it out in the shade, and we will call it a fair share.
May your wells run sweet and your road stay free of serpents. We take no more than we need from our own.
I offered you the courtesy of the road and you spat on it. Then we settle this as the desert settles everything.
The same Eye watches over us both, so we will be gentle about it. Coin for the road, and nobody needs to tell the Tower anything.
Good. Those who fight the same war should not quarrel over trifles. Name a sum and we will call it tribute.
Go on, then. If the captains of the Black Land ask, we never crossed paths.
Then you can explain to the Tower why its servants killed each other in the sand. Spears!
You march in the same war as we do, yet this stretch of desert belongs to the raiders. Every band that crosses it pays, whatever its errand.
So you are no fool. Give us something worth the trouble and we will forget your face before sundown.
Pass, and do not linger near our camps. The sand forgets quickly, and so shall we.
Allies in the war, and still you bare steel at us over a little silver? So be it. Bring them down.
You are far from any friendly banner, and the desert is wide. Empty your packs into the sand and you may live to curse us.
So the proud can bend after all. Give generously, for your life is priced high in Harad.
Crawl back the way you came. The next time the crimson banners find you, there will be no bargaining.
So be it. Ride them down!
Look what the wind blew across our sands. A stranger with full packs and no friends within a hundred leagues. Your gold, all of it.
Fear makes everyone sensible. Pour it out where I can see it, and do not hide a single coin.
Go, and tell whoever you serve that Harad guards its roads with spears. The next toll will be your head.
Then the sun will bleach your bones before the next moon. At them!
Hold your hand! We are only hungry travellers of the sands, the same as you, and nothing in our packs is worth your blood.
Think before you charge. We have both bled under the same sun, and there is easier prey than us on this road.
Have you lost your wits? We fight for the same Eye. Turn your blades on its enemies and leave us be.
Come on, then, if you think the Tower will thank you for it. The raiders of Harad do not die quietly.
You ride against the spears of Harad? Many have tried, and the sand keeps every one of them.
Turn back while you still have water. Our riders know every well and hollow in this waste, and you know none of them.
You fight well, for one who shares our sun and our thirst. Face me alone, and let the winner keep the camp without more of my riders dying.
Enough. The Eye gains nothing if we bleed each other dry. Fight me blade to blade, and the camp goes to whoever is left standing.
The sand has swallowed better than you. Come out from behind your spears and face me alone.
Hold there, ratling. Even kin pay the toll on Gundabad's road, and the chieftain counts every coin.
Sensible. A handful of silver for the chieftain's pot and a bit for us, and nobody tells the wargs you passed.
Go on, then. Tell your own warband the Mountain's toll was fair this time.
Too proud to pay your own? Then the wargs eat well tonight, kin or no kin.
You smell like one of ours, but you walk heavy with plunder. Share it out, or we take the lot.
Good. Half of what you carry, and we forget we saw you creeping past the watch-holes.
Off with you, quick and quiet. Same cold, same hunger, and today you fed us.
Greedy little rat. Hold it down and pick its pockets clean!
We fight for the same Shadow, but this pass belongs to Gundabad. Pay the toll like any other traveller.
A purse of silver will do. Your masters can spare it, and ours never feed us enough.
Pass, then. When the war-drums call, we will remember who paid.
Allies, you say? Allies bleed the same as anyone. Take them!
Stop where you are. We bow to the same dark power, but up here the Mountain bites first. Gold, or we bite.
Fair is fair. A pouch of gold and the food in your packs, and we part as servants of the same Shadow.
Take the low path out and keep to it. The high caves are ours.
No toll? Then you can explain it to the chieftain's trolls. At them!
Look what crawled up from the valleys. Every scrap you carry, sniveller, or we leave you for the crows.
Begging already? Good. All your gold and the boots off your feet, and maybe we let you limp home.
Limp away, then. Tell the valleys Gundabad is coming back for the rest.
Hoped you would say that. Slit their throats and drag the bodies to the caves!
You stand in Gundabad's shadow, worm. Pay the price of the pass, or pay with your hide.
Ha! It squeals for terms. Every coin in that purse, and quick, before the wargs grow bored.
Crawl off and count your fingers. We may come back for them.
Then we take it from your corpse. Wargs, feed!
Hold your blade! The same caves bred us both, so why feed our blood to the crows?
Easy, easy. We only took a few sheep from the valley. Share the meat, and nobody needs to bleed.
Wait! We answer to the same dark lords. Strike us and the Mountain will hear of it.
You turn your blades on Gundabad? Your own masters will hang you for breaking the pact, fool.
Come up the slope then, valley-rat. Every rock up here hides another of us.
Ha! It thinks it can fight Gundabad. We have eaten tougher warriors than you for supper.
You fought through my warren like one of the deep-born. Face me alone, and the stronger of us keeps the cave.
Allies who raid my caves? Fine. You and me, blade to blade, and the winner takes the spoils.
You came all this way into the Mountain's gut. Fight me alone, and I will hang your hide over the door.
Easy there, shipmate. You and I both know the price of bread on a hard road. Share your purse with a few honest corsairs and we all eat tonight.
There, I knew you had sense. Lay it on the barrel head and we will split it fair.
Done, and no hard words between us. If you ever want a berth on a fast ship, ask along the quays of Umbar.
A shame. I would sooner have shared a cup with you than bled you. Cutlasses out!
Hold up, traveller. We are a long way from the sea, the rations are short, and you look like someone who knows how that feels. A little silver keeps us all friends.
Spoken like someone who has stood a hard watch. Make it a fair share and we will not search your packs.
That will see us back to the ships. May the tide run your way, wherever your road goes.
Pity. I took you for one of us. Over the side with you, then!
We answer to no Tower and no White City, and I hear the same is true of you. Still, the coast road takes a toll from everyone who walks it.
Good. Those who bow to nobody ought to be able to strike a bargain. Name the sum.
A clean deal between free blades. If the Captain ever needs hired hands, you know where the ships put in.
Then you are no wiser than the kings who would see us both in chains. Have at them!
Neither the ships of Gondor nor the whips of Mordor have tamed us, and I doubt they tamed you. That makes us near friends, and friends share their silver.
I knew we would see eye to eye. Pay what is fair and we will drink to your health tonight.
Smooth sailing on dry land, then. The corsairs remember who dealt square with them.
So you would rather fight than pay a friend. Then we fight, and the gulls can judge it.
Well now, a fat prize walking the coast road alone. Hand over your purse and your boots, and we may let you keep the rest.
Striking your colours already? Wise. Pile it up here, every coin, and be quick about it.
Off with you, and pray our ships never sight your shore.
Then we take the prize by force, as Umbar always has. Cut them down!
You have the look of someone who has never been robbed by real corsairs. Today you learn how it is done. Everything you carry, now.
Ha! Not even a fight. Throw it all on the sand, and do not make me count twice.
A rich haul. Go and tell your friends the corsairs come ashore whenever they please.
Good, a fight! Our blades have been dry since the last landfall.
Steady, steady! We are only sailors ashore with empty bellies. Keep your sword in its sheath and we will keep ours.
Think twice, friend. We have both known hard roads and harder captains, and there is no gold here worth the bleeding.
You strike at us? We serve no Tower and no White City, and neither do you. Save your steel for those who would chain us both.
Mind your aim! The free blades of this coast have few enough friends without cutting each other down.
Come and try it! Every corsair here learned to fight on a pitching deck, and solid ground makes it easy.
A bold charge against the corsairs of Umbar. The sea has drowned bolder, and we sent most of them there.
Enough of my crew lies bleeding. Face me alone, the way corsairs settle a quarrel, and the winner takes the hold and all in it.
We both keep clear of the great war, so let us settle this freely. One against one, and the cove goes to whoever walks away.
So you found our cove. Draw and face me alone, and we will see which of us feeds the crabs.
Easy now, and keep your hand from your sword. You have the look of someone who has stood a long watch too, so pay what you can spare and we part without blood.
I thought you might see sense. We held the fords while better-fed captains slept, and have nothing to show for it. Name a sum that shames neither of us.
That buys bread and a dry barn for a week. Go safely, and if anyone asks, the road was empty.
Then draw, and may whoever falls be forgiven. I had hoped someone who knows a hard life would spare us this.
Hold there. Ten years we stood against the Shadow on the river, and the Steward's clerks forgot our names. Share a little coin with old soldiers, and we all see tomorrow.
Good. You know what an empty belly does to tired soldiers. Offer something fair and we will not haggle long.
Our thanks. When you sit to your next meal, face west a moment for the comrades we left on the river.
So it comes to blades between the likes of us. Shields together, and finish it quickly.
Stop there, friend of the West. We have no quarrel with any who stand against the Shadow, only with empty purses. Lighten yours a little and go on your way.
Kindly done. We fought for the same cause as you once, before it stopped feeding us. What will you give?
The thanks of Gondor, such as it is from the likes of us. Go on, and may your road stay clear of orcs.
You would rather fight old allies over a few coins? Then guard yourself, and do not expect us to be gentle.
A moment, traveller. We once held the line so that travellers like you could sleep at night. Call it back pay owed, and hand over some silver.
Fair of you. The Steward's treasury never was. Name your sum and we will hear it.
That is more than the Tower ever sent us. Go in peace, and may your own lords pay their soldiers better than ours did.
Then we take it. We are long past caring which side anyone stands on. Steel out!
You there, halt! We may have thrown off the Steward's colours, but we still know an enemy when we see one. Your purse, and quickly.
You would buy your way past us? Fine, an enemy's coin spends like any other. Make it a heavy offer.
Take your road and do not look back. If we meet again, we may not be so hungry.
Good. I have missed fighting an honest enemy. At them!
Halt. Our banners are gone, but our swords still remember the enemy. Empty your saddlebags, or we empty them for you.
So you will pay rather than bleed. Clever. Let us see how much your hide is worth to you.
Done. Ride on before some of us decide the coin was not enough.
Then we finish this as we did in the old days in Ithilien. No quarter for those who cross us!
Wait! We have bled for the same lands you ride through. Must it end with us killing each other?
Put up your swords. We are tired, hungry and few, and none of us wants to die on a muddy road for nothing.
Steady! We once fought beside allies such as you against the Dark Lord. Is this how the Free Peoples repay us?
Turn back. We still know how to hold a shield wall, and you will break on it before you break us.
So the enemy comes looking for us now. We held against worse on the river, and we will hold here.
Come on, then. Gondor taught us to fight before it forgot us, and we remember every lesson.
Enough of this slaughter between soldiers. Face me alone, sword to sword, and let my company live or die by how it ends.
I was a captain once, with a banner and a good name. Meet me alone and let the outcome settle this, as was done in the old wars.
You have come far into our camp, enemy. I will meet you alone, blade to blade, and show you what a captain of the Tower was worth.
Well met, cousin of the deep places. Even kin pay toll on this road, though we take less from you than from the rest. Open your purse.
Good. No need for axes between those who know the dark under the mountains. Weigh out a fair share.
The debt is settled and no beard is bloodied. Go, and do not speak of the Blacklocks in your own halls.
So you would raise an axe against your own blood over a little gold. Then you are no better than the ones who drove us out.
Stop, kin. The halls that turned us out have done the same to others, maybe to you. Share your gold with the outcast, and we part friends.
Spoken like one who knows what it is to lose a hall. Show us the gold and we will be fair with it.
May the Maker keep you, since the Maker has forgotten us. Walk on, and stay clear of the eastern passes.
Then let the old grudge between our houses grow one line longer. Axes!
We bend the knee to no king, and you keep out of the Dark Lord's war as we do. That makes us neighbours, and neighbours pay toll.
A neighbourly answer. Show us the coin, and do not hide the good pieces at the bottom.
Counted and found honest. Go, and if anyone's soldiers come asking, you met no one in these hills.
We kept out of everyone's wars to keep our gold. Do not think we will lose it to you now. Shields locked, axes high!
You there. You owe nothing to the great powers, much like us. Still, the road is ours, and the road takes its share in gold.
Sensible. Those who stay out of the great war have to look after their own purses. What have you got?
A clean bargain. Remember that the Blacklocks dealt fairly with you, and deal fairly with us next time.
Your mistake. We have outlasted kings and worms, and one stubborn traveller will not trouble us long.
Hold! You march under a banner, and banners mean wars that were never ours. Pay for passing through our hills, and pay well.
So the proud will pay after all. Weigh it out, and we will tell you when it is enough.
Taken and written in the book. Go, and tell your lords the hills of the east answer to no one.
Good. Our axes have gone too long without work. Break them!
Stand fast, stranger. The Blacklocks keep long memories for those who serve the great powers. Your gold, or your blood on the stones.
Coin from an enemy is still coin. Set it on the rock where we can see it.
That pays for this road and nothing more. Cross our hills again and the price will be dearer.
Close ranks. We stopped counting enemies the day our halls were taken, and we will not start again with you.
Stay your hand! We are of the same stone and the same blood, whatever our banners say.
Think on it before you strike. The halls cast us out, but we still swing axes as well as any who stayed.
Back off. We have no master and no quarrel with you, and you would do well to leave it so.
Attack the Blacklocks in our own hills? The stones here have drunk better blood than yours.
Come then. Every axe in this clan has a grudge to spend, and you will do.
Strike, if you dare. The Blacklocks have stood against greater armies than yours and are still here.
You found our hold, kin. Then let it be settled the old way, you and I alone, axe to axe, with the clan as witness.
Far enough. I am chief of the Blacklocks, and I will meet you alone before my clan, if you have the stomach for it.
You have broken into the last hall the Blacklocks own. Stand before me alone and earn the right to take it.
Stand still. You walk with the light step of our own, but exiles cannot live on remembered songs, so your silver comes to us.
You remember that the woodland shares what it has. Half of what you carry will do, and we will not count the rest.
It is done, and without grief. If the King's wardens ask, you met no one beneath these boughs.
So be it. Let the trees see which of us forgot the old songs first.
Rest your bow, wanderer. We were cast out of the King's halls long ago and our courtesy went with us, so set down your silver.
There is still some sense in the old blood. A fair share and no more, for we have no wish to strip one of our own.
Go, and keep to the paths where the light still reaches. Some of us remember how to be kind, though it comes slowly now.
Then let the trees bear witness. We will sing for you when it is over.
Halt there. You owe nothing to any great banner and neither do we, which makes this a plain matter of silver.
Sensible. Lay a fair portion on that stone, and we will judge whether it is fair.
Enough. Go your way, and if the Elvenking's wardens find you, you saw only birds in the branches.
You bargain with blades, then. We have lived too long to fear one more fool in the dark.
Neither the King nor the Shadow rules this part of the forest. We do, and the toll is paid in silver.
No great power stands behind either of us, so let us keep this small. A third of your purse will settle it.
That will serve. Follow the stream until the trees thin, and do not leave the water after dusk.
A poor choice. Your bones will be green with moss before the moon is full.
You walk this forest uninvited, under a banner we have no love for. Pay for every step, or lie here until the leaves cover you.
Then pay well, for we have little mercy left for the cause you serve. All the gold you carry, and quickly.
Go before we think better of it. If your banner passes beneath these trees again, no gold will save it.
Then the forest will have you. Loose!
The spiders took our kin and the King took our homes, so we take what we please from strangers. Coin now, or blood.
A coward's bargain, but we will take it. Empty your purse to the last coin and step back from it.
Begone. The forest forgets nothing, and neither do we.
Then learn why travellers fear the dark under the trees. Shoot!
Would you hunt your own beneath the trees? Lower your blade, and we will forget you ever came.
We were sent out of the King's halls once already. Must you finish what the King began?
We have no quarrel with you and no master to send after you. Ride on and leave us to the dark.
Careful. We know every root and hollow of this forest, and you know none of them.
Come, then. We have fought worse than you in this darkness, and outlived them all.
Strike if you dare. This forest has swallowed armies, and it will hardly notice you.
Enough of our blood has stained these roots. Face me alone, one exile against one wanderer, and let the trees judge between us.
You found our hollow, which few ever do. Meet me alone beneath the great oak, and whoever falls, the rest go free.
I have kept this hollow since long before you drew breath. Face me alone if you have the nerve, and let the others watch.
Hungry, hungry. You are one of us, so we ask nice once. Give food and shiny, or we eat yours.
Good, good. Throw down the meat bag and a fistful of coin. Den shares, den lives.
Go, go. No whips out here, no masters. Come back when you are hungry too.
Not sharing? Then the den eats you, bones and all!
We smell it on you, the whip-scars and the hunger. Out here nobody owns us. Pay the den or bleed for it.
Yes. Half your bread, all your shiny. Then we let you run.
Gone now. Tell the other runaways the den is fat this season.
Thinks it is bigger than us! Bite it! Biggest gets first pick!
Stop! Your masters in their towers mean nothing here. In the wild we eat what we catch, and we caught you.
Meat and coin, lots of it. Drop it on the ground and back away slow.
Run back to your masters, then. Tell them the dens bow to nobody.
No pay? Good! Coin is cold and flesh is warm. Get it!
You march for the Shadow? We do not. Out here only the strongest rules, and the strongest says pay.
Leave the pack beasts and the purse. We are not greedy, only hungry.
Walk now, while the den is busy eating. Do not look back.
Then we take beasts, purse and you. Rip!
Food! Food walking in the wild! Throw down everything, or we pull you down and eat.
It wants to bargain. All the food, all the shiny, every last crumb, and maybe we only bite a little.
Run, run far. Next time the den is hungrier.
Good, it fights! Hot blood tastes better!
No road here, no lord, no law. Just the den, and the den wants what you carry.
Clever. Empty the sacks, drop the blades, and crawl past on your belly.
Crawl on, then. We know your scent now, and we will smell you coming.
Too slow to pay, too slow to run. Pull it down!
No, no! Same blood, same hunger! Why hunt your own when the valleys are full of fat prey?
Put it down! We ran from the whips and the pits, same as any of us would. Let the den be.
Hah, the Shadow sends its hounds after us now? We bow to no tower. Come and bleed.
Leave the den alone! We took nothing of your masters'. Only sheep, only stragglers.
You come to the den? Good. The den was hungry, and now the food comes by itself.
Wait! Wait! Take bones, shinies, anything! Just do not burn the den!
You smell strong. The den follows the strongest, so fight me alone, and whoever stands keeps the den.
No master I bow to sent you here. Fight me, just you and me, and the den eats the loser.
Biggest in the den, me. You want the den, you beat me, one on one, teeth and iron.
Easy now, we were farmers before the war burned the barns. Hand over a little coin and nobody bleeds on this road.
You look like you have known lean winters too. A few coins and a loaf if you have one, that is all we ask.
That will keep the children fed a while. Go on, and may the road treat you better than it treated us.
Then you are no better than the raiders who took everything. Get at them!
Stop there, friend. The war took our fields and our lord forgot us, so the road is the only field we have left to reap.
We are not thieves by trade. Give what you can spare and we will call it fair.
Thank you, truly. Watch the ford ahead, other raiders have been about.
We buried too many this winter to fear one more grave. Come on, then!
Hold up! Nobody rides to avenge anyone out here, and we have not eaten in two days, so give us your coin.
No need for blades. Some silver and whatever food you carry, and we will let you be.
Go on, then. Mind the burned village past the hill, there are worse than us sleeping in its cellars.
Hunger makes a body brave. At them!
We care nothing for whose banner you follow, or whether you follow any. An empty belly takes no side, so pay up.
That is more like it. Half of what jingles in your purse, and keep the rest for your own troubles.
Fair enough. The roads have gone bad everywhere since the Shadow rose, so keep your eyes open.
Stubborn, are you? We have nothing left to lose but our lives, and those are not worth much.
Your war burned our homes and left us to starve by the roadside. Now you can pay for some of it.
Pay, then, and pay heavy. Every coin you hand over is one your lords owe us.
Take your road and your war away from here. We have nothing left for either.
Then we take it from your corpse! For the farms they burned!
Armies marched through our valley and left only ash, and you ride under their banners. Empty your purse.
Smart. Everything you carry, the food first, then the coin.
Get out of our sight before we think better of it. Hunger makes poor judges.
Better to die fighting than starve in a ditch. Have at them!
Mercy! We are only hungry folk who lost our farms, the same as half the realm.
Wait, we are no raiders! Just poor farmers driven off our land, and we would sooner run than fight you.
We have nothing worth taking, only rags and an empty pot. Leave us be and go your way.
Come no closer! We starved through one winter already, and we will not die easy in this one.
Back off! Your armies took our harvest, and you will not take our lives as well.
Go on, then, cut us down. It is quicker than hunger.
